newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Tractebel says may sue Hungary over hikes.
newsitem.headline: Tractebel says may sue Hungary over hikes.

text.p: Belgian utility group Tractebel said on Monday it was considering suing Hungary's government over an energy pricing policy which it says prevents it making a profit on its investment in a Hungarian power station.

"We are considering taking legal action," Tibor Kuhl, Tractebel's director for its Hungarian operations told Reuters, adding that the company may also seek to sell back to the state the 47 percent stake in the Dunamenti oil-fired power station it bought at the end of 1995 for $141 million.

"The reason we are considering (both actions) is that, based on the current government's (pricing) proposals, we will make a loss next year while the prevailing law states that the government minister must set prices which cover costs and ensure a profit," he said.

The government announced 10 days ago retail hikes of 24.5 percent for electricity and 18.8 percent for gas but did not define the margins which would be granted to energy producers and distributors, in which Western utilities invested over $2 billion last year.
The Hungarian Energy Office said the government would announce the margins for suppliers and distributors in mid-December.

The announcement of the hikes followed the cancellation of price rises for October after the rejection of recommendations by the Hungarian Energy Office of increases rumoured to be 39 percent for electricity and 25 percent for gas.

Companies such as Gaz de France and German electricity giant RWE, which bought into the gas distribution network, were promised an eight-per-cent return on investment from January 1997 and have expressed concern that the January hikes would be too little too late to generate such profits.
Kuhl said Tractebel, which was also promised eight per cent on its investment in Dunamenti, had the additional problem of not being able to pass on changes in fuel prices to the customer.

"Unlike the distributors which have a fixed margin between a fixed wholesale price and a fixed retail price, nobody can fix our margin because we purchase 65 percent of our heavy fuel on the free market," he said.
"On the one side our eight percent is not secured and on the other huge losses can be incurred by ministers setting an energy price and not being able to fix the market price."
Kuhl said the government must make allowances for heavy fuel price fluctuations and periodically adjust consumer prices so that these fluctuations are passed on to the customer.

"We need a quarterly revision of the price whereby every quarter we will calculate the difference between the estimated cost as per the government price and actual cost and the difference must be compensated, as in other countries," he said.

Kuhl said the that an adequate framework had been set up through legislation and the mandate given to the Energy Office for setting the rules. By rejecting those rules last year and fixing consumer prices before settling all the costs the government had broken its promises, he said.
"The underlying law says you have to analyse the costs and then the end-price, not the other way round," he said.
"We want the government to wake up and come up with a new proposal that abides by the rules."
